rv.q: The production does full justice in its portrait of complicated, imperfect and doggedly hopeful motherhood.
Terry is astonishingly good as Mother Courage.
It's a hardcore performance in a hardcore show that won't be to everyone's taste.
Michelle Terry, whose superpower is her rare ability to slip into any part and seem born to play it – and this really is a winning turn.
As that other former Globe artistic director Mark Rylance did before her, Terry knows exactly how to play this wraparound space so as to draw in all spectators and her command is a delight to watch.

It doesn’t help that this production, designed by takis, lacks visual flair. A battered sofa dominates one side of the stage; a walkway that projects into the space normally occupied by groundlings provides room for a pit into which corpses are unceremoniously tipped from time to time.
It's a powerfully robust performance, starting off jocular but failing to hide much of the tragedy and fear within.
A topical translation of one of the great anti-war dramas proves another smart programming choice from Terry's Globe, and continues its rich vein of form.
Dark, distressing, funny and thoroughly entertaining, this production is a powerful and emotionally charged experience.
With such a towering central performance, perhaps there is yet a chance I shall become a devotee of this difficult-to-enjoy play.

For all its ambition and Terry's remarkable energy in portraying a remarkably energetic woman, the vision of this production never resolves into a clear picture, too sharp at some times, too fuzzy at others.
Together these elements combine to make for a theatrical experiment that finds some novelty in creative risks, but not enough to make the production feel truly insightful or a knockout.
It feels like a key work under Terry’s leadership.
This lively production brings out Brecht's innate theatricality as well as conveying his political message, in a show that is thoroughly entertaining and at times surprisingly moving.

cn.t: Michelle Terry commands attention in this loud, brash Brecht production that finds a surprisingly natural home at the Globe, though some question whether the venue's inherent intimacy undermines Epic Theatre's essential alienation.
